title: Sonos spent two years on wireless home audio instead of starting with speakers
dek: Sonos's founding team decided it shouldn't compete with Bose on speakers, but instead solve the unsolved problem of wirelessly syncing digital music across the whole house—a choice that sustained the company for the next twenty years.
why: Traces Sonos's full journey from initial sketch through confrontation with Steve Jobs, to iPhone apps and standalone speakers as a rescue strategy—useful for understanding the decision-making logic of early hardware startups. The middle section features detailed engineering work; skip if you prefer to focus on the strategic story.
who: Entrepreneurs and product managers interested in smart hardware startup history, product strategy tradeoffs, and differentiation tactics against incumbents.
skip: Skip 20:07–22:12 for detailed mesh network debugging; jump ahead to 23:16 for the antenna breakthrough.

points.h: The first decision is not what to build, but what to refuse
points.body: McFarlane and the team explicitly abandoned speaker manufacturing during the planning phase because premium audio companies like Bose had already locked down that market, and a small startup couldn't compete. Instead, they discovered that no audio company had solved the problem of 'wirelessly sending music to every room without a tangle of wires.' So they bet everything on that gap. This choice determined Sonos's product form for the next twenty years: only amplifiers and networking, letting users bring their own speakers.

points.h: Distributing intelligence to each device beats centralizing it in one place
points.body: The engineering team faced a choice when designing the system architecture: create a central brain to command all amplifiers, or turn each amplifier into a mini-computer that could think for itself. The centralized approach was simpler—just one computer to fix—but if the brain failed, the whole system crashed. The team chose the harder but more resilient path: distributing intelligence across every device. This early architectural choice proved correct and laid the foundation for the later mesh network.

points.h: Military mesh networks solved what home Wi-Fi couldn't
points.body: Engineers found that home Wi-Fi in 2003 was fragile enough that a single boarding pass printing job could jam the network, let alone support multiple speakers in sync. The solution came from mesh networking, developed by the military years earlier: no single hub, devices talk to each other, blow up one node and the rest keep communicating. Sonos brought this battlefield technology into the living room, so speakers didn't depend on home Wi-Fi to talk to each other but instead used their own internal wireless mesh.

points.h: A supplier spotted the basic problem the engineers missed
points.body: The prototype could sync music playback but couldn't transmit a signal ten feet. The team drove three hundred miles to Silicon Valley with the prototype in a cardboard box to get a supplier's help. The supplier opened the machine, glanced at it, and said one word: antenna. Sonos had forgotten to put an antenna in a system designed to transmit through walls. It's a reminder that spending too long on complex technical problems makes you overlook the basics—sometimes an outside view is worth more than an inside expert.

points.h: When Apple entered the same market, Sonos picked differentiation over direct competition
points.body: In 2004, Apple announced AirPort Express at the same conference, also focused on wireless music, making Sonos look like it could be stillborn. But Apple's system needed to plug into existing speakers, required separate hardware for each room, couldn't sync across devices, and required you to stay at the computer to change songs. Sonos came with a remote control, amplifiers with built-in speaker-driving power, and all receivers in one mesh network that could play the same song across rooms in sync—something Apple couldn't do. When a startup faces a giant entering the market, you don't have to slug it out in their strength; give customers a reason to choose you instead.

points.h: Pushing back launch six months beats shipping a broken product
points.body: In the summer of 2004, Sonos promised to ship for the holidays that year at $1,200. As the deadline approached, engineers reported honestly that the problems couldn't be fixed in time. McFarlane didn't hesitate; he pushed launch to spring of the next year—a huge risk for a company with no product, no revenue, running on the founder's own money. But he feared that running out of money mattered less than putting a broken product on the market and destroying his name first.

points.h: Financial crisis forced an iPhone app that accidentally revived sales
points.body: During the 2008 financial crisis, the number of pings from registered Sonos devices dropped to near zero, exposing a cliff-edge collapse in sales. By then, engineer Nick Millington's secret project group had built an iPhone app that could replace Sonos's proprietary remote control, which sold for nearly $400, letting users operate the system free on their phones. The irony: four years earlier, Steve Jobs had threatened to sue over the Sonos remote looking like an iPod. Now Apple's iPhone had become the tool that saved Sonos's life.

points.h: McFarlane's misjudgment of Alexa nearly cost the company
points.body: When Amazon Echo launched, McFarlane wasn't worried about voice recognition—he tried it and thought the technology had overpromised for years. But in the 2015 holiday season, Amazon sold roughly a million Echo units, equivalent to one-quarter of Sonos's annual sales. Only then did McFarlane realize that if Amazon kept that pace, Sonos's market position wouldn't last long. The company shifted strategy, but instead of building its own voice assistant, it integrated third-party ones like Alexa and Siri—a pivot that directly led to 2016 layoffs.
